author: interplains
body:
# Zero Breach Toolkit

A free, open-source check for traces of known mercenary spyware (Pegasus, Predator,
Graphite, Candiru and others) on computers, Android phones and iPhone backups.

- **Read-only.** It does not modify source evidence or system settings. It writes only
  temporary database snapshots and the reports you ask for.
- **No network requests during a scan.** It never looks up spyware addresses and has no
  upload feature. Python network calls are blocked and redirected paths are refused. This
  is not an operating-system network sandbox; see [PRIVACY.md](PRIVACY.md).
- **States its limits.** Every report says what was found, how strong the evidence is, and
  what could not be checked. A clean result is never presented as proof that you are safe.

Made by archivegenocide. Built on [Zero Breach](https://github.com/interplains/zero-breach).

> **If you think you are being targeted right now, get expert help first.** You do not
> need to run this tool before asking. Journalists, activists, human-rights defenders and
> civil society can contact the
> [Access Now Digital Security Helpline](https://www.accessnow.org/help/) (free, 24/7,
> many languages) or [Amnesty International's Security Lab](https://securitylab.amnesty.org/get-help/).

---

## Step-by-step guide (no technical experience needed)

You do not need a GitHub account or any technical knowledge. You need a Windows or Mac
computer and about 20 minutes. Phones are checked by connecting them to the computer.

**What do you want to check?**
[This Windows computer](#windows) ·
[This Mac](#mac) ·
[An Android phone](#android-phone) ·
[An iPhone](#iphone)

### Windows

**Set up (only the first time)**

1. Go to [python.org/downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/) and click the yellow
   **Download Python** button. Open the downloaded file.
2. On the first screen of the installer, **tick "Add python.exe to PATH"** at the bottom,
   then click **Install Now**. Wait until it says "Setup was successful".
3. On this page, click the green **Code** button near the top, then **Download ZIP**.
4. Open your **Downloads** folder, right-click **Zero-Breach-Toolkit-main.zip** and choose
   **Extract All**, then **Extract**.

**Run the check**

5. Close your web browsers and chat apps (Chrome, Edge, WhatsApp, Signal…).
6. Open the **Zero-Breach-Toolkit-main** folder (if there is another folder with the same name
   inside, open that one too), then the **scan** folder, and double-click **run-scan.cmd**.
   If Windows shows a warning, click **Run** (or **More info**, then **Run anyway**).
7. A menu appears. Type the number next to **Update the indicator lists** and press Enter,
   then type `y` and press Enter. When it finishes, press Enter.
8. Press Enter again to start **This computer - standard check**. It takes about 15 minutes.
9. Read the result at the end (see [What the result means](#what-the-result-means)). A copy
   is saved in the **findings** folder inside Zero-Breach-Toolkit-main.

### Mac

**Set up (only the first time)**

1. Go to [python.org/downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/), click **Download Python**,
   open the downloaded file and follow the installer. When it finishes, open **Finder →
   Applications → Python 3** and double-click **Install Certificates.command** (without it,
   updating the indicator lists fails).
2. On this page, click the green **Code** button, then **Download ZIP**. It appears in your
   **Downloads** folder as **Zero-Breach-Toolkit-main** (if it is still a .zip file,
   double-click it).
3. Open **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Full Disk Access**, click **+**, choose
   **Applications → Utilities → Terminal**, and turn it on. Without this, macOS hides
   Safari's records from the check.

**Run the check**

4. Close your web browsers and chat apps.
5. Open **Terminal** (press Cmd+Space, type `Terminal`, press Enter). Copy this line, paste it
   into Terminal and press Enter:
   ```
   cd ~/Downloads/Zero-Breach-Toolkit-main && python3 -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py
   ```
6. A menu appears. Type the number next to **Update the indicator lists** and press Enter,
   then type `y` and press Enter. When it finishes, press Enter.
7. Press Enter again to start **This computer - standard check**. It takes about 15 minutes.
8. To keep a copy of the result, type `3` and press Enter, then type `.` (a full stop) and
   press Enter. It is saved in the Zero-Breach-Toolkit-main folder with the date and time in
   its name, so every check gets its own file. Type `0` to finish.

### Linux

**Set up (only the first time)**

1. Open a terminal (on most desktops, press Ctrl+Alt+T). Python 3 is usually already
   installed; check with `python3 --version`. If it is missing, install it with your
   package manager, for example `sudo dnf install python3` (Fedora),
   `sudo apt install python3` (Ubuntu, Debian, Mint) or `sudo pacman -S python` (Arch).
2. On this page, click the green **Code** button, then **Download ZIP**. In your
   **Downloads** folder, right-click the zip and choose **Extract Here**, so that you have a
   folder named **Zero-Breach-Toolkit-main**.

**Run the check**

3. Close your web browsers and chat apps.
4. Copy this line, paste it into the terminal and press Enter:
   ```
   cd ~/Downloads/Zero-Breach-Toolkit-main && python3 -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py
   ```
5. A menu appears. Type the number next to **Update the indicator lists** and press Enter,
   then type `y` and press Enter. When it finishes, press Enter.
6. Press Enter again to start **This computer - standard check**. It takes about 15 minutes.
7. To keep a copy of the result, type `3` and press Enter, then type `.` (a full stop) and
   press Enter. It is saved in the Zero-Breach-Toolkit-main folder with the date and time in
   its name, so every check gets its own file. Type `0` to finish.

You do not need `sudo` to run the check. It reads your own account's records; if you run with
`sudo`, it may look at the root account's browsers instead of yours.

### Android phone

First do the **Set up** steps for [Windows](#windows) or [Mac](#mac) above.

**On the phone**

1. Open **Settings → About phone** and tap **Build number** seven times, until it says you are
   a developer. (On Samsung: **Settings → About phone → Software information → Build number**.)
2. Go back to **Settings**, open **Developer options** (often under **System**) and turn on
   **USB debugging**.
3. Connect the phone to the computer with a USB cable that carries data (some cables only
   charge). Unlock the phone. When it asks **Allow USB debugging?**, tick **Always allow** and
   tap **Allow**.

**On the computer**

4. Start Zero Breach (Windows: double-click **run-scan.cmd**; Mac: step 5 of the Mac guide).
5. In the menu, type the number next to **A phone** and press Enter, then type `2` (**Collect
   from an Android phone connected by USB now**) and press Enter.
6. Press Enter to save the collection on your Desktop, then type `YES` and press Enter.
7. The collector asks a few questions. Use the arrow keys and Enter to answer:

   | It asks | Choose |
   |---|---|
   | Backup | **Only SMS** |
   | Download copies of apps | **Only non-system packages** |
   | Remove copies of apps signed with a trusted certificate | **No** |
   | Intrusion Logs | **No** |
   | Hash files | **No** |
   | Anything else | **No** |

8. If the phone shows **Back up my data**, tap it (leave the password empty). Keep the phone
   unlocked until the collection finishes.
9. The check starts by itself and shows the result.
10. When you are done, turn **USB debugging** off again on the phone.

### iPhone

First do the **Set up** steps for [Windows](#windows) or [Mac](#mac) above.

These steps work the same way for an **iPad**. The check runs on a computer, not on the iPhone
or iPad itself: iOS and iPadOS do not let any app read other apps' data, so the device is backed
up to a computer and the backup is checked there.

1. **Make a backup on the computer.** Connect the iPhone with a cable and tap **Trust** on the
   phone.
   - Windows: install **Apple Devices** from the Microsoft Store, open it and select the iPhone.
   - Mac: open **Finder** and select the iPhone in the sidebar.
2. Choose **Back up all of the data on your iPhone to this computer**, tick **Encrypt local
   backup**, choose a password you will remember, and click **Back Up Now**. Wait until it
   finishes.
3. **Open the backup folder:**
   - Windows: press **Windows key + R**, paste `%USERPROFILE%\Apple\MobileSync\Backup` and press
     Enter.
   - Mac: in Finder, choose **Go → Go to Folder**, paste
     `~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup` and press Enter.

   Inside is a folder with a long name of letters and numbers: that is your backup.
4. Start Zero Breach. In the menu, type the number next to **A phone**, press Enter, type `1`
   and press Enter.
5. **Drag the backup folder** (the one with the long name) into the Zero Breach window and press
   Enter.
6. When asked whether the backup is password-protected, type `y` and press Enter, then type the
   backup password (nothing appears while you type) and press Enter.

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| `'python' is not recognized` or nothing happens on Windows | Run the Python installer again, choose **Modify**, and make sure **Add Python to environment variables** is ticked. Restart the computer. |
| `No such file or directory` on a Mac | Type `python3 -X utf8 ` (with a space at the end) in Terminal, then drag the file `zero-breach-toolkit.py` from the toolkit's `scan` folder into Terminal and press Enter. This works from any folder. |
| `Bad CPU type in executable`, or trying to run it on an iPad or iPhone | The check cannot run on an iPad or iPhone. Back the device up to a Windows PC or Mac (the iPhone steps above work for an iPad too) and check the backup on that computer. |
| A folder named `candiru` in the download | That is part of the toolkit: `third_party/candiru` holds the published detection rules for Candiru's spyware, not the spyware. Leave it in place; if it was deleted, download the toolkit again. |
| "encrypted iPhone backups require optional cryptography" after installing it | It went into a different Python. Install it with the same command you start the check with (`python3 -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements-backups.txt` on a Mac), from the toolkit folder. |
| `command not found: python3` | Install Python from python.org (step 1), then close and reopen Terminal. |
| A match inside an ad blocker such as uBlock Origin | Fixed in 0.1.15: ad-blocker filter lists contain these domains in order to block them, so a match in the browser's copy of a list is now a note, not a finding. Update to the latest download. |
| `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` on Windows (updating the lists or collecting from an Android phone) | Open **PowerShell** and run `Invoke-WebRequest https://github.com -UseBasicParsing \| Out-Null`, then try again: Windows downloads some certificates only when first needed. If it still fails, pause your antivirus's HTTPS scanning ("web shield") for a moment. |
| Updating the indicator lists fails on a Mac (`CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED`) | Open **Finder → Applications → Python 3** and double-click **Install Certificates.command**, then update again. Full Disk Access does not affect updating. |
| Android: the collector finds no phone | Unlock the phone, use a different cable or USB port, and check **Allow USB debugging** was accepted. Unplug and plug in again. |
| iPhone: "wrong password" | Use the password chosen when **Encrypt local backup** was first turned on. If it is forgotten, it can be reset on the iPhone (Settings → General → Transfer or Reset iPhone → Reset → Reset All Settings), then make a new backup. |
| Safari "could not be checked" on a Mac | Give Terminal Full Disk Access (Mac step 3), close Terminal, open it again and run the check again. |

Still stuck? Ask in the [issues](https://github.com/interplains/Zero-Breach-Toolkit/issues)
(do not post your report there; it contains private details).

### What the result means

- **"No known indicators found"**: nothing from the published spyware lists was found in
  the places the tool could check. It is not proof that the device is clean: read the list
  of places that could not be checked.
- **"Something matched"**: this means *look closer*, not *you are infected*. Do not delete
  anything and do not visit the address it names. Keep the report and contact the
  [Access Now Digital Security Helpline](https://www.accessnow.org/help/) (free, 24/7).
- The report never leaves your computer unless you send it to someone yourself.

---

## What it checks

### Windows

No administrator rights are needed.

| Where | What it looks for |
|---|---|
| Browsers at their default locations: Chrome, Edge and Brave (including beta, dev, canary and nightly channels), Chromium, Vivaldi, Opera, Opera GX, Arc, Yandex; Firefox, LibreWolf, Waterfox, Floorp, Zen, Pale Moon, Tor Browser | indicator addresses in history, cookies, connection records, HSTS, bookmarks, downloads, site storage and caches, per profile |
| Desktop apps with a built-in Chromium browser | supported history, cookie and storage records; raw app web caches are skipped and reported as a gap |
| Downloaded files | the website each file came from (the "Mark of the Web" stamp) |
| The Win+R box | commands people were tricked into pasting by fake "verify you are human" pages |
| Antivirus status and Microsoft Defender history | registered antivirus products and their reported status; past Defender detections, protection-off events and added exclusions |
| PowerShell log | scripts that named a spyware address, or downloaded and ran code |
| Programs listed by Windows | existing files named in the shim cache and the Windows 11 launch list, compared with published sample fingerprints; not a complete execution history |
| Prefetch and Amcache | supported Prefetch executable-name records and Amcache file inventory; the program files they name are never opened |
| Selected user folders | fingerprints of candidate files, within size and directory limits |
| DNS cache, DNS history, hosts file, COM and startup/task/service registrations | known indicators in supported network and persistence records; not a full persistence audit |

A Prefetch match (`execution-record`) does not identify the file's contents or full path;
an Amcache match (`inventory-record`) does not prove execution or that the file still
exists. Locked or unsupported records are gaps.

Antivirus status comes from Windows Security Center, including third-party products such
as Bitdefender that register there. An active registered product puts an old Defender-off
event in context; it does not mean protection is off now. Registration is not a health
test; some enterprise products do not register, and unavailable status is a gap. A desktop
app such as Slack is listed because its web records were checked, not because it is
suspicious.

The default hash check covers `.dll`, `.exe`, `.sys`, `.ocx`, `.cpl`, `.scr`, `.tmp`,
`.dat`, `.bin` and `.ax` files up to 120 MiB in selected folders, skipping cache and
dependency directories. Computer checks can find published infrastructure or file traces;
they cannot tell whether a phone is infected.

### macOS and Linux

The same browsers are checked at their default locations, plus common Snap and Flatpak
packages and Firefox's newer `~/.config/mozilla` profile folder on Linux. On a Linux desktop
in another language, the translated Downloads, Desktop and Documents folders are found from
`user-dirs.dirs`. File fingerprints, separate browser cache locations and bounded saved-record
checks run without administrator access.

- **Safari (macOS):** history and profile databases, open and iCloud tabs, the URL cache,
  WebKit's tracking-prevention list, cookies, HSTS records, bookmarks, downloads, Top Sites
  and recently closed tabs.
- **Startup configuration:** on Linux, standard autostart `.desktop` entries, systemd units
  and immediate `.conf` overrides, cron configuration and scheduled script directories; on
  macOS, standard LaunchAgent and LaunchDaemon property lists. A launch item's program is
  compared as an executable path and, by its file name, as a process name.
- **Shell and logs (both):** standard shell startup files, saved Bash/Zsh/fish history
  (including macOS Terminal's per-session history in `~/.zsh_sessions`), the hosts file and
  readable current text system logs. Paths inside `$( )` and backticks are recognised. Large
  history and log files are limited to recent records; the omitted part is a gap.

These read saved configuration, not which jobs are enabled or ran. Network strings are
references; exact known executable paths in supported launch configuration can be
findings, with activation and execution unverified.

File checks also cover extensionless files, executables, native libraries and scripts in
selected application, user and temporary folders (120 MiB limit). Windows-only live checks
do not run here; copied Prefetch and Amcache files can still be selected in targeted mode,
though compressed Prefetch needs Windows.

### Desktop apps

Apps with a built-in Chromium browser are found by their folder contents under AppData
(Windows), Application Support (macOS) or the user and Flatpak configuration folders
(Linux), including apps whose own folder is a Chromium profile, such as Signal on macOS.
The search has no fixed depth limit; it is bounded by folder count and time, and reaching
that bound is reported as a gap.

### Android

The tool reads a collection made with [AndroidQF](https://github.com/mvt-project/androidqf);
it never talks to the phone itself. It checks:

- installed and running apps, their fingerprints and signing certificates;
- the install history, so an app that was installed and later removed still shows;
- system records, logs and crash records;
- supported, already decrypted intrusion logs: DNS lookups, TCP connection attempts and
  process-start events (a connection attempt does not prove success);
- links in SMS and MMS messages, from the SMS backup AndroidQF offers to take;
- apps installed outside an app store, with what they can do (read SMS, use the
  microphone, read notifications, resist uninstalling) and when they arrived;
- signs of a modified phone: unlocked bootloader, debug build, security protection off.

It recognises the collection's own traces (USB debugging, the debugging shell's
permissions) and does not report them as suspicious.

### iPhone

Local Finder, Apple Devices or iTunes backups (encrypted or not), extracted file systems
and sysdiagnose archives. See
[Checking local iPhone evidence](#checking-local-iphone-evidence).

### Indicators

About 12,400 published indicators from 29 sources: Amnesty International's Security Lab,
the [Mobile Verification Toolkit](https://github.com/mvt-project/mvt-indicators) project,
the Citizen Lab and Echap's stalkerware research, and a hand-curated set from Citizen Lab
reports (Candiru / DevilsTongue and Paragon's Graphite) with every line cited. The curated
set works offline; `--update` downloads the rest from a fixed list of official sources.

---

## Install and run

You need Python 3.8 or newer ([python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/); on Windows,
tick "Add python.exe to PATH" when installing). No administrator rights and no extra
packages. On macOS and Linux type `python3` instead of `python`.

1. **Get the toolkit.** On GitHub choose **Code → Download ZIP** and extract it, or:
   ```
   git clone https://github.com/interplains/Zero-Breach-Toolkit.git
   ```
2. **Open a terminal in the toolkit folder.** Windows: open the extracted
   folder (`Zero-Breach-Toolkit`, or `Zero-Breach-Toolkit-main` from a ZIP), click the address bar, type `powershell` and press
   Enter. macOS: open Terminal, type `cd ` (with a space), drag the folder into the window
   and press Enter. Run every command below from this folder.
3. **Recommended: download the latest indicator lists.** This is optional and is the only
   step that uses the internet; the checks themselves never do. Without it only a small
   built-in set is used. Repeat it every few weeks.
   ```
   python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --update
   ```
4. **On a Mac, give Terminal Full Disk Access first** (System Settings → Privacy & Security
   → Full Disk Access → add Terminal, then reopen it). Without it macOS blocks Safari's
   records and some folders, and the report lists them as not checked.
5. **Close your browsers and chat apps**, then run the check. A menu opens; press Enter for
   the standard check of this computer.
   ```
   python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py
   ```
   On Windows you can instead double-click `scan\run-scan.cmd`. It saves the readable and
   JSON reports in a `findings` folder next to the toolkit.

Reports contain private details from your computer; keep them out of shared and synced
folders. Useful options:

```
python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --quick                     # faster: skips file fingerprints
python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --phone "FOLDER"            # a phone collection or backup
python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --json report.json          # machine-readable report
python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --share-json summary.json   # minimal summary for sharing
```

Put folder paths in quotes, especially if they contain spaces. On Linux or macOS,
`sh scan/run-scan.sh` takes the same options.

### Verify what you run

The project is anonymous, so do not take its word for anything. Verification rests on what
you can reproduce.

Running from source, as above, means every line the tool executes is in the clone: nothing
is compiled and nothing is fetched in order to run.

The single-file `zero-breach-toolkit.py` attached to a release is generated from the same
source. Rebuild it from the release's tag and compare:

```
git checkout v0.1.15
python build/bundle.py
python -c "import hashlib; print(hashlib.sha256(open('dist/zero-breach-toolkit.py','rb').read()).hexdigest())"
```

For v0.1.15 the file is 986,053 bytes, SHA-256
`4ebe1f3043e5efd056e201143bed8d4a44c3b937afde19f7b89e240cbf4a32f9`. The size and SHA-256
published with each release are authoritative. The build is deterministic, so a matching
rebuild means the published file contains that source and nothing else. Releases are also
GPG-signed; see [docs/VERIFYING.md](docs/VERIFYING.md).

There is no signed Windows program, and none is planned while the project stays anonymous:
code-signing certificates require a named legal identity. An `.exe` you build yourself with
PyInstaller is unsigned, has no download reputation and is not byte-reproducible, so
SmartScreen will warn, some antivirus products will flag it, and the comparison above does
not apply. Running from source avoids all of that.

### Checking an Android phone

1. On the phone, turn on *Developer options* (Settings → About phone → tap *Build number*
   seven times), then turn on *USB debugging*.
2. Connect the phone by USB and tap *Allow* when it asks about this computer.
3. Download and run [AndroidQF](https://github.com/mvt-project/androidqf/releases) on the
   computer. Answer its questions like this:

   | AndroidQF asks | Answer |
   |---|---|
   | Take a backup of the device? | Only SMS |
   | Download copies of all apps or only non-system ones? | Only non-system packages |
   | Remove copies of apps signed with a trusted certificate? | No |
   | Take the Intrusion Logs? | No, unless you turned on Intrusion Logging |
   | Hash files on the device? | No (Yes also checks file fingerprints, but it is slow and can stop the collection on some phones) |
   | Browser history / Magisk modules? | No |

   On the phone, confirm the backup with *Back up my data*.
4. AndroidQF saves a `.zip` next to itself. Extract it.
5. From the toolkit folder, check the extracted folder (keep the quotes):
   ```
   python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --phone "PATH TO THE EXTRACTED FOLDER"
   ```
   Or run the tool with no options, choose *A phone*, and drag the folder into the window.
6. Turn USB debugging off again.

The collection holds private information about the phone. Keep it on your computer.

Use `--phone-guide android` for preparation steps and `--phone FOLDER --preview` to list
which artifacts are available. For an AES-encrypted `backup.ab`, add `--backup-password`;
the password is asked for privately at the terminal and never appears as an argument or in
a report. Age-encrypted acquisition archives must first be decrypted with the owner's
identity using the separate age tool; this scanner does not launch it.

**Guided acquisition (experimental).** `--collect-android LOCAL_OUTPUT_FOLDER` downloads
official AndroidQF v1.8.3, checks its pinned SHA-256, asks for the device owner's explicit
consent and runs the collector's interactive prompts. After a successful plaintext
acquisition it extracts the archive locally and checks the collection. Acquisition changes
phone state and saves private records; it is separate from read-only scanning.

This is the only point at which the tool runs a program it did not ship:

- the asset name and expected digest are fixed in the source;
- the file is fetched over HTTPS from the publisher's release, with redirects limited to an
  allow-list, and hashed while downloading;
- if the digest does not match, acquisition is refused and nothing is executed;
- the collector is written to a temporary directory and run directly, not through a shell,
  with `ADB_`, `ANDROID_ADB_`, `LD_` and `DYLD_` variables removed and `PATH` reset to the
  system directory, then deleted when the command finishes;
- nothing is downloaded or run unless you invoke the command and confirm consent.

The pinned digest verifies the publisher's release bytes; it is not an independent audit of
the collector. The publisher ships the Windows build unsigned, so a browser download shows
the usual "not commonly downloaded" warning and SmartScreen prompts on first run. If you
prefer, install AndroidQF yourself, follow the five steps above and skip this command.

`--age-recipient-file PATH` supplies public age1 recipients (private identity files are
refused). When encryption is requested, a plaintext result is refused. An encrypted result
must have a supported age envelope and no unexpected extra files, but these format checks
cannot authenticate it or verify the recipient. It is saved for separate decryption; the
command succeeds without producing a scan or an all-clear. After a failure, check the
reported folder: original or partial records are kept and may be unencrypted.

### Checking local iPhone evidence

1. Make a local backup with Finder (Mac) or Apple Devices / iTunes (Windows). Tick
   *Encrypt local backup*: encrypted backups include more of the records this tool checks.
2. Find the backup folder (one per device, with `Manifest.plist` inside): on a Mac
   `~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/`, on Windows
   `%USERPROFILE%\Apple\MobileSync\Backup\`.
3. From the toolkit folder (keep the quotes; leave out `--backup-password` if the backup
   is not encrypted, and the password is asked for privately):
   ```
   python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --phone "PATH TO THE BACKUP FOLDER" --backup-password
   ```

`--phone-guide ios` and `--phone-guide android` print these steps in the terminal.

Encrypted backups need the optional `cryptography` package already installed in your Python
environment; nothing is installed automatically. Install it from the toolkit folder with the
same command you start the check with: `python3 -m pip install --require-hashes -r
requirements-backups.txt` on a Mac or Linux, `python -m pip ...` on Windows (every package
pinned by version and hash). If the check still says it needs cryptography, it was installed
for a different Python on the same computer. The supported version is cryptography 50.0.2, which needs Python 3.9 or
later. Intel Macs get 48.0.1, the last release published for them; its remaining advisories
concern certificate checking, which this tool does not use.

For evidence you already have, use `--phone ROOT --ios-input filesystem` for an extracted
file system, or `--phone PATH --ios-input sysdiagnose` for a directory or TAR/TAR.GZ archive.
Both are also in the phone menu. This does not acquire a device.

It reads messages (SMS, iMessage, WhatsApp), Safari and other browsers, data-usage
processes, app records, permissions, calls, calendar, interactions, Shortcuts,
configuration profiles, analytics and diagnostics (shutdown logs, crash and memory reports,
running processes, installation logs). Local browser visits are separated from synced or
imported ones; unknown origin stays a reference with a gap. Unusual paths alone are leads.

Committed SQLite WAL records, including encrypted backup sidecars, are validated and
replayed on temporary copies. JSON findings keep source hashes and record locators. While a
table's row index is readable, an unreadable message, visit or process row is skipped and
later rows are still checked; repeated gaps are grouped. Unsupported encodings or schemas,
damaged WALs, record caps, unavailable protection classes and encrypted `Manifest.db` WALs
are gaps. The test suite covers the table layouts
of iOS 15, 16, 17 and 18. See [docs/IPHONE.md](docs/IPHONE.md) for exact support and limits.

### Choosing the scope

- `--scan-type default` uses the computer checks and file candidates supported on your platform.
- `--scan-type full` also reads desktop-app raw web caches and hashes all file extensions
  in the usual roots, including subdirectories normally skipped. It is broader, not a scan
  of every drive, account or artifact. The 120 MiB file limit remains.
- `--scan-type targeted --target PATH` reads only the selected files, directories, drives
  or browser profiles; repeat `--target` for several. Selected files are hashed whatever
  their extension, within the same size and access limits. Copied Prefetch/Amcache files
  inside the selection are also read. Live registry and log checks are outside this scope.
- `--scan-type browser` reads only this account's browser profiles and desktop apps with a
  built-in Chromium browser (history, cookies, site storage, caches and connection records)
  against every loaded list, including ad-campaign addresses. Large caches can take several
  minutes. Files, startup entries, DNS, registry and system events are not read.
- `--preview` prints the proposed scope without scanning. File hashing reports progress.
  Ctrl+C stops the scan and reports what was collected, with an incomplete-coverage gap.
- `--extended-windows` adds existing Sysmon and Security process events. It does not enable
  logging or elevate privileges. If access is denied, a second run from an administrator
  terminal can read what the ordinary account could not.

On Windows, saved console and Explorer input is also read; it does not prove that anything
ran. Startup checks interpret recognisable batch commands, Internet Shortcut URLs and literal `.lnk` target and
argument metadata, without resolving or opening the target; anything they cannot interpret
is a gap. Related-record groups link the same indicator across artifacts with their dates
and original grades; they do not claim a causal attack sequence. Publisher validity,
platform and withdrawal labels are shown as context.

See [the coverage table](docs/COVERAGE.md) before relying on a particular check.

### Start menu and follow-up

Running the tool in a terminal without choosing a check shows a menu. Enter starts the
standard check; 0 quits without scanning. The same menu offers a full check, a
browsers-only check, selected files or folders, or a phone collection. Scripts with
non-interactive input do not see it; `--no-menu` turns menus off.

The browsers entry also offers a test of whether your browser blocks ads. That test only
works inside a browser, so the tool asks first and then opens the ArchiveGenocide test page
in your default browser. The browser goes online for it; the tool does not. See
[PRIVACY.md](PRIVACY.md).

After a menu-selected check you can inspect findings and references, review gaps and next
steps, save reports, or prepare a private evidence bundle. `--post-menu` offers the same
after a command-line scan. The report is shown before those choices. The Windows launcher
keeps prompts visible and saves both readable and JSON reports.

`--report PATH` saves the readable report, independently of `--json` and `--share-json`.
Reports never replace an existing file inside a selected evidence folder, a selected input
file, or the app data and app cache folders where desktop apps keep the records the scan
reads. Choose a new filename. No baseline snapshots are kept.

### Private evidence handoff

`--evidence-bundle PATH` creates a new, **unencrypted** private ZIP with the full JSON
report, readable report, minimal sharing summary and an integrity manifest. Repeat
`--evidence-file PATH` to add original local files you choose. Report text never chooses
files to copy, and nothing is uploaded or sent to a helpline.

```text
python scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --scan-type targeted --target SUSPICIOUS_FILE --report report.txt --json report.json --evidence-bundle evidence.zip --evidence-file SUSPICIOUS_FILE
```

`SUSPICIOUS_FILE` is the path of one file; `--evidence-file` takes files, not folders.

The archive is previewed before it is created, never overwrites an existing file, and is
limited to 128 originals of up to 64 MiB each and 256 MiB in total. It records SHA-256
hashes, tool version, scope, times and fingerprints of the indicator sets used. Hashes show
later integrity, not authenticity to the original device. Originals are copied at export
time and may differ from what was scanned; live databases may need their sidecar files
selected too. Use the minimal summary for first contact, and share the full archive only
through a secure route agreed with the recipient.

---

## Reading the result

The report starts with a short summary: what was found, what it means, what to do, and what
could not be checked. The evidence follows.

- **Findings** carry an evidence grade. "A known spyware file is on this machine" or "an
  app researchers name is on this phone" is strong. "A saved web page mentions the address"
  is weak, and is usually an article about the spyware. The grade, not the number of
  matches, decides what to do.
- **Worth a look** lists things the tool cannot judge on its own (a sideloaded app, a
  command that downloaded code, an antivirus exclusion), each with its usual harmless
  explanation. They are not findings.
- **In time order** lists every dated finding and item.
- **What could not be checked.** Read this part. A check that could not run has not
  cleared anything.

Exit codes for scripts:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | no actionable matches and no recorded coverage gaps |
| `1` | setup, argument or output error |
| `2` | a match beyond a saved reference |
| `3` | no actionable matches, but checks or indicator sources were incomplete |
| `4` | the start menu was closed without scanning (no verdict or report) |

Reference-only matches stay visible and return `0` or `3`, depending on gaps. No exit code
proves a device is safe.

## What it cannot do

- It only finds published indicators. New or unpublished spyware will not be found.
- Spyware is often rebuilt for each target, and many traces expire within weeks.
- An Android check sees only what the collection contains; an iPhone check sees only
  supported artifacts in the local evidence supplied. Neither is a full phone examination.
- It does not replace a forensic examination by experts. If you are worried, ask for help.

## Privacy

`--update` downloads indicator sources. The separate `--collect-android` command downloads
a pinned official collector after consent. Ordinary scans stay offline. Full reports can
contain usernames, profile names, file paths, browsing details, SMS senders and message
excerpts; keep them private. `--share-json summary.json` writes counts, scope labels, the
verdict and fixed advice, and leaves out artifact text, indicator values and dates. It is an
initial summary, not forensic evidence; review it before sharing. See [PRIVACY.md](PRIVACY.md).

## For scripts and assistants

`--describe` prints, as JSON, every check the tool runs, what each reads and cannot see,
the exit codes and the rules for relaying a result. `--json` writes a machine-readable
report that marks the fields to relay to the person, the next steps that may be given, and
which fields hold untrusted text from the scanned machine. See
[scan/CONTRACT.md](scan/CONTRACT.md).

A [skill file](skills/zero-breach-toolkit/SKILL.md) is included for assistants that support
skills: add the `skills/zero-breach-toolkit` folder to the assistant's skill directory, or
have it read that file. It covers scope selection, encrypted-backup prompts, offline
operation, report interpretation and evidence privacy. Nothing is installed automatically.

## Tested platforms

Windows, macOS, Linux, Android (AndroidQF collections) and iPhone (local backups). See
[docs/COVERAGE.md](docs/COVERAGE.md) for what each check reads and its limits. Built-in
readers share one registry for platform selection, coverage descriptions and the
single-file build; see [scan/READERS.md](scan/READERS.md) to add one.

## Where the code is

There is no `src` folder; the code is under [`scan/`](scan/):

- [`scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py`](scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py): the entry point you run.
- [`scan/zbtriage/`](scan/zbtriage/): the scanner (indicator loading, the network block,
  reporting). The package keeps the project's earlier name so existing installs keep working.
- [`scan/zbtriage/modules/`](scan/zbtriage/modules/): one file per check (browsers, Windows
  records, macOS and Linux, Android, iPhone, file fingerprints).
- [`scan/tests/`](scan/tests/): the test suite.
- [`build/bundle.py`](build/bundle.py): builds the single file attached to each release from
  this source (see [Verify what you run](#verify-what-you-run)).

## Credits

Indicators are the work of Amnesty International's Security Lab, the Citizen Lab, the MVT
project and Echap.

## Licence

Code, including the generated scanner: Apache License 2.0 ([LICENSE](LICENSE)). The curated
indicator files in `iocs/` and generated indicator exports in `dist/`: CC0 1.0, public
domain ([iocs/LICENSE.md](iocs/LICENSE.md)). Optional bundled research rules keep their own
licences in [third_party/candiru](third_party/candiru/README.md). Indicator lists downloaded
by `--update` remain under their publishers' terms and are not part of this repository.

title: Jakeschincariol/replica-skill
author: Jakeschincariol
body:
# The Replica skill

Eleven Claude skills that clone any app. Free, MIT, no signup, no API key,
nothing to connect.

One reverse-engineers the app you want to clone. One rebuilds it. One tests it
for bugs. And one is the Entrepreneur: it reads what the app's users hate and
fixes it in yours, so you have an app you can sell.

In between, the others plan the stack and the database, rebuild the design
system, wire up auth and payments, score your clone against the original, give
it a name and a brand of its own, write the landing page and the store
listing, and put it live on your domain.

**It rebuilds what an app does, never what it owns.** Features and flows,
clean-room style. Not its code, its logo, its copy or its content. The
fine print is at the bottom, and the skills enforce it.

## Install

Paste this into Claude:

```
https://github.com/Jakeschincariol/replica-skill

install skill
```

Or as a plugin, in Claude Code:

```
/plugin marketplace add Jakeschincariol/replica-skill
/plugin install replica-skill@replica-skill
```

Claude Code namespaces plugin skills, so installed as a plugin they show up as
`/replica-skill:replica-recon` and so on. Copy the folders instead if you want
plain `/replica-recon`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Jakeschincariol/replica-skill.git
cp -r replica-skill/replica-* ~/.claude/skills/
```

Project-local instead of global: copy the same folders into your repo's
`.claude/skills/`. No Claude Code at all? Paste any single `SKILL.md` at the
top of a chat and it runs as a mode. You lose the Python tools, but the
method works.

The tools need Python 3.8 or newer. Nothing to pip install.

## The eleven

| command | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/replica-recon` | Reverse-engineers any app: screens, flows, components, data model. From public pages, screenshots, store listings and your own account. |
| `/replica-architect` | Plans the stack, database schema and API for your clone. |
| `/replica-design` | Rebuilds the design system: colours, type, spacing, components. As tokens, with your own assets. |
| `/replica-build` | Rebuilds the app screen by screen from the recon map. |
| `/replica-backend` | Auth, database, payments and integrations. |
| `/replica-test` | Clicks through every flow and tests it for bugs. |
| `/replica-diff` | Compares your clone against the original. A parity score and what is missing. |
| `/replica-entrepreneur` | Reads what the app's users hate in real reviews and turns it into fixes and a positioning angle. |
| `/replica-brand` | Names and rebrands your version so it is yours. |
| `/replica-launch` | Landing page, pricing and App Store listing. |
| `/replica-deploy` | Ships it live on your own domain. |

## How to use it

Run them in order. Each one reads what the last one wrote, in a `replica/`
folder in your project.

```
recon -> architect -> design -> build -> backend -> test -> diff -> entrepreneur -> brand -> launch -> deploy
```

An example: cloning a scheduling app, the kind where you share a link and
people book a time with you.

1. **`/replica-recon`** with the app's URL. It reads the help center, the
   pricing page, the store listing and public walkthroughs, and you click
   through your own account with it. Out comes `replica/recon.md`: 18
   screens, 7 flows (guest books a meeting, host sets availability, guest
   reschedules...), the components, an inferred data model (users, event
   types, availability, bookings) and `features.csv`. The partner
   marketplace is marked out of scope: that is their network, not a feature.
2. **`/replica-architect`** picks Next.js, Postgres, Stripe and Resend, writes
   the schema (with a constraint so two guests can never book the same slot)
   and orders the build: the booking flow end to end first.
3. **`/replica-design`** measures the screenshots into tokens: colour roles,
   type scale, 8px spacing, the date picker and slot button specs. Open
   icons, an open font, your own words.
4. **`/replica-build`** builds the shell, then the booking flow, then every
   screen with all its states, ticking off `features.csv` as it goes.
5. **`/replica-backend`** adds sign up, Google Calendar through Google's own
   API with your keys, Stripe for paid bookings, reminder emails.
6. **`/replica-test`** writes a test plan from the 7 flows, Playwright specs
   for the happy paths and edge cases (time zones, a slot taken mid-booking,
   double submit), and logs bugs by severity until no S1 or S2 is open.
7. **`/replica-diff`** scores it. Features 86, all must-haves done, booking
   page layout 91. Missing: round-robin for teams, the website embed.
8. **`/replica-entrepreneur`** reads 140 real reviews across the App Store,
   G2, Capterra and Reddit. Top complaints: per-seat price jumps, no text
   reminders, guests confused by time zones. Each with counts and linked
   quotes. Fix plan: flat pricing, SMS reminders, a time zone confirm step.
   Angle: booking links for small teams that hate per-seat pricing.
9. **`/replica-brand`** names it (with the trademark and domain checks to
   run), gives it a new palette, a logo brief and a voice, then sweeps the
   codebase until nothing of the original is left.
10. **`/replica-launch`** writes the landing page around the angle, sets
    pricing against the original's public page, and lints the store listing.
11. **`/replica-deploy`** runs the preflight (tests, parity, sweep, listing),
    sets up production, gives you the DNS records for your domain, and ships
    it when you say go.

You can also run any one on its own. `/replica-entrepreneur` on an app you
are only thinking about cloning is a good way to find out if you should.

## The tools

Six of them, all standard-library Python. None touch the network.

```bash
python3 replica-diff/imgdiff.py original.png clone.png --out diff.png   # layout diff, ignores colour
python3 replica-diff/parity.py replica/features.csv                     # parity score + missing list
python3 replica-entrepreneur/reviews.py replica/reviews.csv             # what users hate, ranked, linked
python3 replica-design/contrast.py replica/design/tokens.json           # WCAG contrast on your tokens
python3 replica-brand/sweep.py . --avoid "Original App"                 # anything of the original left?
python3 replica-launch/listing.py replica/launch/listing.json           # store limits + copycat checks
```

**`imgdiff.py`** reads PNGs with no libraries, turns both screenshots into
edge maps and compares where things are, so your new colours do not count
against you. It tells you which regions differ, in the original's pixels.

**`parity.py`** weights must, should and could, counts partial as half, and
never scores what you left out on purpose or what you added. Missing
must-haves means not shippable, and it says so.

**`reviews.py`** drops every review without a link. Every quote it prints is
copied from a row you gave it, with that row's URL. Themes with under three
reviews or one source are marked thin.

**`sweep.py`** finds the original's name, domain and colours anywhere in your
code, including inside identifiers like `OriginalAppEmbed`, and blocks the
deploy until it is clean.

**`listing.py`** checks App Store and Google Play limits, ranking claims in
the title, wasted keyword characters, and the original's name anywhere in
your listing.

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

## Fine print

**It rebuilds functionality and UX patterns, clean-room style.** It studies
what the app does and how people move through it, then writes everything
fresh. It never copies the target's source code, proprietary assets, logos,
trademarks, copy or private APIs.

**It only reads what you are allowed to read.** Public pages and your own
account. It never scrapes behind a login or against a site's terms, never
logs into anyone else's account, and never gets past a paywall. If your
account's terms forbid using it to build a competitor, it says so and sticks
to public sources.

**It always rebrands before launch.** New name, new palette, new logo, new
words. `/replica-deploy` will not ship until the sweep is clean.

**"Clone any app" means the features and the flow.** Not the content, the
network or the licences an app owns. You can rebuild a music app's player,
playlists and sharing. You cannot clone its catalogue.

**No guarantee of a "perfect" clone.** Results depend on how complex the app
is. A booking tool is weeks. A spreadsheet engine is not. `/replica-recon`
sizes it honestly before you start, and `/replica-diff` gives you a real
number, not a vibe.

**The Entrepreneur never makes things up.** No invented reviews, quotes or
numbers. Every claim has a link, and the sample size is stated.

**Check before you sell.** Run the trademark checks `/replica-brand` lists,
read the terms of anything you used, and talk to a lawyer before launch if
there is money on the line. This is not legal advice.

## Files

```
replica-recon/         SKILL.md, recon-map.md, features.csv (the matrix template)
replica-architect/     SKILL.md, architecture.md
replica-design/        SKILL.md, tokens.json, contrast.py
replica-build/         SKILL.md
replica-backend/       SKILL.md
replica-test/          SKILL.md, test-plan.md, bug-report.md, e2e.example.spec.ts
replica-diff/          SKILL.md, imgdiff.py, parity.py
replica-entrepreneur/  SKILL.md, reviews.py, themes.json
replica-brand/         SKILL.md, sweep.py
replica-launch/        SKILL.md, listing.py, listing.example.json
replica-deploy/        SKILL.md, preflight.md
tests/                 the tests for every tool
```

Your own files live in `replica/` in your project. The skills read each
other's.

Made by Jake Schincariol, [opusjake.ai](https://opusjake.ai). Siblings:

title: marcelodosreis/sassy
author: marcelodosreis
body:
Sassy

Welcome to **Sassy**, a powerful template generator designed to accelerate the development of Micro-SaaS applications. Built with **Next.js 15**, **TypeScript**, **TailwindCSS**, **Supabase**, and **Stripe**, Sassy provides a robust foundation for building subscription-based services with integrated authentication, subscription management, and payment processing. | **Feature** | **Status** | |-----------------------------------------|------------| | OAuth Authentication (Google, FB, Twitter) | ✅ | | Subscription & Billing (Stripe) | ✅ | | Free Trial Periods (Stripe) | ✅ | | Billing Portal (Stripe) | ✅ | | Webhooks for Stripe Events | ✅ | | Subscriptions & Payments API Routes | ✅ | | User Authentication (Supabase) | ✅ | | E-Mail (Mailgun) | ✅ | | Personalized Dashboard | ✅ | | Responsive Design + Landing Page | ✅ | | Logs & Monitoring (Datadog) | ✅ | You can learn more about the other features by visiting the following documentation page: [Sassy Documentation](https://github.com/marcelodosreis/sassy/blob/develop/docs). We are constantly improving Sassy with new features to make it even more powerful. You can find the current roadmap and planned features on our [Feature Roadmap](https://github.com/marcelodosreis/sassy/blob/develop/docs/feature-roadmap.md) ## Architecture and Structure Sassy's architecture is designed to streamline the rapid development of Micro-SaaS applications by providing essential features like user authentication, subscription management, and seamless payment processing. The project structure is clean and organized to help developers get started quickly while maintaining flexibility and scalability. ### Project Structure: ```bash src/ ├── app/ # Main logic and core functionality of the application ├── components/ # Reusable UI components ├── constants/ # Global constants and configurations ├── contexts/ # React contexts for global state management ├── hooks/ # Custom React hooks ├── libs/ # Third-party libraries and utilities ├── pages/ # Next.js pages corresponding to routes │ └── api/ # API routes for backend functionality ├── services/ # External API integrations and services ├── styles/ # TailwindCSS configuration and custom styles ├── utils/ # Utility functions and helpers └── middleware.ts # Middleware for request processing ``` ### Integration with Supabase and Stripe: - **Supabase** is used for user authentication and real-time database management. The `subscriptions` table is created to store subscription-related data for each user. - **Stripe** is integrated to handle payment processing and subscription plan management. ### SQL Script for Creating the `subscriptions` Table in Supabase: ```sql CREATE TABLE subscriptions ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(), user_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES auth.users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, stripe_subscription_id TEXT UNIQUE, plan TEXT CHECK (plan IN ('free', 'starter', 'creator', 'pro')) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'free', status TEXT CHECK (status IN ('active', 'canceled', 'past_due', 'incomplete', 'trialing')) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active', current_period_start TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, current_period_end TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW() ); ``` > **Note:** Since subscription data is sensitive, ensure that **Row Level Security (RLS)** is disabled for the `subscriptions` table. ### Environment Configuration: The environment variables are configured to integrate Sassy with Supabase and Stripe. Make sure to update the values accordingly. ```env NEXT_PUBLIC_PROJECT_URL= NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY= NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL= NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY= NEXT_PUBLIC_DATADOG_APPLICATION_ID= NEXT_PUBLIC_DATADOG_CLIENT_TOKEN= SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY= STRIPE_SECRET_KEY= STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET= DATADOG_SECRET_KEY= MAILGUN_SECRET_KEY= MAILGUN_SECRET_DOMAIN= ``` > **Note:** Replace the above values with your own Supabase and Stripe keys. ## Key Features - **Authentication with Supabase:** Utilize Supabase for user authentication, providing a secure and scalable login system. - **Subscription Management with Stripe:** Easily manage different subscription plans, handle payments, and track user subscriptions with Stripe integration. - **Responsive Design with TailwindCSS:** The application uses TailwindCSS for styling, ensuring a modern and responsive design out of the box. - **Built-in API Routes:** Ready-to-use API routes for managing subscriptions, payments, and user data. - **OAuth Support:** The app supports OAuth login via **Google**, **Facebook**, and **Twitter**, providing users with a seamless authentication experience. --- ## Webhook Listener for Stripe To handle incoming webhooks from Stripe (such as subscription updates, payment failures, etc.), Sassy includes a script for listening to Stripe webhooks: ```bash pnpm stripe:listen ``` This script connects your local environment to Stripe and listens for events like **invoice.payment_succeeded**, **invoice.payment_failed**, and more. It will automatically trigger the corresponding handler in your application to process the events. > **Note:** When using this in your development environment, make sure you have the Stripe secret key and webhook secret configured in your `.env.local` file. --- ## OAuth Authentication Sassy comes with built-in OAuth authentication support for popular platforms such as **Google**, **Facebook**, and **Twitter**. The authentication flow is fully integrated with Supabase, ensuring a secure and seamless experience for users. ### Dependencies: - OAuth SDKs for Google, Facebook, and Twitter to provide login functionality. With **OAuth**, users can authenticate with their preferred social media accounts, reducing friction in the signup/login process. OAuth tokens are securely managed by Supabase, and user data is synchronized across both Supabase and your application. > **Note:** The OAuth login functionality is already set up and fully supported out of the box. If you're using different authentication providers, you can easily extend this functionality by following the Supabase OAuth documentation. --- ## Setup Instructions ### 1. Install Dependencies Ensure that you have **pnpm** installed. If not, install it globally: ```bash npm install -g pnpm ``` Then, install the project dependencies: ```bash pnpm install ``` ### 2. Set Up Environment Variables Create a `.env.local` file in the root directory of the project and add the necessary environment variables (as provided in the **Environment Configuration** section). ### 3. Run the Development Server Once the environment is set up, start the development server: ```bash pnpm dev ``` The application will be available at `http://localhost:3000`. ### 4. Database Configuration To set up your Supabase project, run the provided SQL script to create the `subscriptions` table in your Supabase database. ### 5. Stripe Integration Make sure your Stripe API keys are correctly set up. You can test the payment processing using Stripe’s test keys in a sandbox environment. --- ## Development vs Production Environments For **development** and **production**, Sassy uses separate Supabase projects to ensure a clean and isolated environment. This allows you to safely test changes in the development environment without affecting live data in production. > **Note:** Ensure that you configure your `.env.local` with the correct Supabase project URL and keys for each environment. --- ## Conclusion Sassy provides a solid foundation for developing subscription-based Micro-SaaS applications. By leveraging the power of **Next.js**, **Supabase**, **Stripe**, **OAuth**, and **TailwindCSS**, you can rapidly build and deploy secure and scalable applications. Whether you're just starting a new SaaS product or iterating on an existing idea, Sassy makes it easy to focus on what matters most: delivering value to your users. --- For more information on integrating **Stripe**, **Supabase**, and **OAuth**, refer to the official documentation: - [Stripe Documentation](https://stripe.com/docs) - [Supabase Documentation](https://supabase.com/docs) - [OAuth Integration Guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-helpers/oauth) - [Sassy Integration with Datadog](https://github.com/marcelodosreis/sassy/blob/main/docs/datadog.md)

title: s87343472/backlink-pilot
author: s87343472
body:
# Backlink Pilot v3

An AI Agent playbook for paced directory and list backlinks: free / free-queue by default, treat reciprocal links, badges, and ownership checks as configurable costs, and grow a reusable site library.

[中文](README.zh.md) · [Docs home](docs/index.md) · [Full guide](docs/guide.md) · Agent runbook [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) · Legacy CLI branch [`old`](https://github.com/s87343472/backlink-pilot/tree/old) (v2.1)

---

## What it is

**Backlink Pilot** is an **AI Agent playbook** (Grok Bot and others) for directory / list outreach — not a black-box “submit hundreds in one command” script.

| Version | Contents |
|---------|----------|
| **v3 (this branch `main`)** | Strategy tiers, daily caps, email loop, `/links`, library ledger, risk notes; human README + agent runbook [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) |
| **v2.1 (branch [`old`](https://github.com/s87343472/backlink-pilot/tree/old))** | Legacy CLI: OpenClaw / Claude Code / bb-browser / Playwright toolkit |

**In the repo:** method docs, empty templates (product card with media fields, library CSV, `/links` example, [assets](docs/assets.md) checklist), historical `targets.yaml` (**unmaintained**).  
**Not in the repo:** runnable batch-submit CLI (see `old`), real submit logs, passwords / cookies, filled directory lists.

---

## What it's for

After you ship an indie product, you often want links from **directories, free-queue launches, and resource / awesome lists**. Forms differ; many need login, captcha, scheduling, and email verification. The hard part is **policy judgment + email loop + pacing**, not filling one form.

This project helps you:

1. **Set rules** — Conservative / Standard / Aggressive; default **Standard** (free & free-queue; optional badge and domain ownership OK; skip paid and required reciprocals by default)
2. **Pace work** — about **2–4 real submissions per day**; scout in bulk, submit slowly
3. **Reuse** — a library ledger of site attributes and per-product status so the next product hits validated sites first
4. **Hand off cleanly** — humans handle DNS/meta, domain mail, paid/tier exceptions; agents research, submit, click verifies, and bookkeep
5. **State the risk** — directory link value varies; volume ≠ rankings (see Disclaimer below)

It is **not** a ranking promise, a link-buying guide, or a tutorial on evading search enforcement.

---

## How to use

### For humans

**Shortest path:**

1. Read [Notes](#notes注意事项) and [Disclaimer](#disclaimer免责声明) (full text: [docs/disclaimer.md](docs/disclaimer.md))
2. Copy [templates/product.example.yaml](templates/product.example.yaml) for your product (**location and email must match Terms / Privacy**)
3. **Prep a media pack:** square logo (prefer transparent), OG (~1200×630), desktop/mobile screenshots, optional banner / promo video, plus short/long slogan variants. Checklist: [docs/assets.md](docs/assets.md); put paths on the product card
4. Copy [templates/library.schema.csv](templates/library.schema.csv) locally (e.g. `library.filled.csv`); **do not commit filled ledgers**
5. Optionally add a `/links` page ([templates/links-page.example.md](templates/links-page.example.md); docs: [reciprocity](docs/reciprocity.md))
6. Paste [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) (or the English block in [templates/agent-prompt.md](templates/agent-prompt.md)) into the Agent’s system / project instructions; set tier (recommend Standard) and daily cap 2–4
7. Give the Agent an inbox for signup verifies; keep domain `support@` for yourself

**What humans must do (the Agent should stop and ask):**

| Task | Why |
|------|-----|
| DNS TXT / page meta ownership | Touches your domain or production site |
| Verify links in a domain mailbox | Agent often cannot read that inbox |
| Paid boost / Featured | Forbidden on Standard by default |
| Required reciprocal, badge-required-to-submit, upvote-for-credits | Policy exceptions |
| Change location / email after rejection | May touch legal pages |
| Captcha / 2FA / unauthorized bulk GitHub PRs | Account & compliance |
| Final logo / OG / screenshots / video | Design & brand; Agent only checks and uploads |

Setup: [docs/agent-setup.md](docs/agent-setup.md) · Grok Bot case (fictional Northstar Notes): [docs/grok-bot.md](docs/grok-bot.md) · Full guide: [docs/guide.md](docs/guide.md)

Want local Chrome scripts / old adapters? Check out [`old`](https://github.com/s87343472/backlink-pilot/tree/old) — [migrating-from-v2](docs/migrating-from-v2.md).

### Verified agents

**Only Grok Bot is verified on v3 (`main`)** (through 2026-10). Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, DeepSeek-family agents, Cursor Cloud Agent, ChatGPT / Custom GPT alone, OpenClaw, and similar runtimes have **not** had a systematic smoke test of “read AGENTS.md + templates → submit / email loop.”

Docs are designed to be agent-agnostic (markdown runbook + templates), but **unverified ≠ proven to follow them**. Criteria, full matrix, and how that differs from branch `old` (v2.1 CLI toolkit targets): [docs/verified-agents.md](docs/verified-agents.md).

If you tried any Agent with this playbook (including ones still listed as unverified), please open an [Issue](https://github.com/s87343472/backlink-pilot/issues) or PR: could it follow `AGENTS`, where did it stick, and did it respect the daily cap and human gates? If it meets the verification criteria, send a PR per the checklist at the end of [docs/verified-agents.md](docs/verified-agents.md) to mark that Agent verified (no filled ledgers, real site lists, passwords, or cookies). Doc, template, and translation fixes are welcome too — see [docs/contributing.md](docs/contributing.md).

### For agents

**Canonical runbook: [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md)** (Chinese: [`AGENTS.zh.md`](AGENTS.zh.md)). Summary:

| Item | Default |
|------|---------|
| Tier | **Standard** |
| Real submits / day | **2–4** (scouting does not count) |
| Allow | free, free-queue; optional badge for dofollow; meta/DNS verify after human adds tokens |
| Skip | paid; required reciprocal; upvote-for-credits; dead; fit mismatch |
| Roles | Research tags → submit (prefer HTTP/API) → email triage → local CSV |
| Media | Before submit, verify product-card paths; if required image/video missing → skip or ask ([assets](docs/assets.md)) |
| Ask human | Paid, required reciprocal/badge, upvote-for-credits, legal location, domain mail, DNS/meta, rejection resubmit, unauthorized bulk PRs, new design exports |
| Report | Counts + reasons for submitted / pending / skipped; no third-party URL spam unless asked |

Product fields: [product-template](docs/product-template.md) · Library: [library](docs/library.md) · Email: [email](docs/email.md) · Funnel: [funnel](docs/funnel.md)

### Doc map

| Doc | Topic |
|-----|--------|
| [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) | Agent runbook |
| [docs/guide.md](docs/guide.md) | Full playbook |
| [docs/strategy.md](docs/strategy.md) | Tiers & pace |
| [docs/reciprocity.md](docs/reciprocity.md) | Reciprocal · badge · `/links` |
| [docs/library.md](docs/library.md) | Library ledger |
| [docs/assets.md](docs/assets.md) | Logo / OG / screenshots / video / slogans |
| [docs/verified-agents.md](docs/verified-agents.md) | Which Agents are verified (Grok Bot only for now) |
| [docs/disclaimer.md](docs/disclaimer.md) | Full disclaimer |
| [docs/troubleshooting.md](docs/troubleshooting.md) | Pitfalls (anonymized) |

---

## Notes（注意事项）

1. **Pace:** Prefer about 2–4 real submissions per day; do not treat tens or hundreds of signups/submits in a day as recommended.
2. **Tiers:** Public docs default to **Standard**; skip required reciprocals; optional badges and ownership verify are OK. See [strategy](docs/strategy.md).
3. **`/links`:** Host reciprocals and badges on a dedicated page, not in homepage body copy; required reciprocals only after you raise the tier.
4. **Library:** Keep filled CSVs local; this repo ships an empty header only. `targets.yaml` is a historical idea pool — **not guaranteed submittable**.
5. **Honesty:** Accurate product copy; matching categories; location / entity / email consistent with legal pages or expect rejection.
6. **Media:** Most sites want logo / OG / screenshots and sometimes video; wrong ratio or size gets rejected. Humans export; Agents pick files per site. See [docs/assets.md](docs/assets.md).
7. **Secrets:** Do not commit passwords, cookies, verify tokens, or filled ledgers (see `.gitignore`).
8. **GitHub lists:** Read CONTRIBUTING first; no bulk PRs without the account owner’s authorization.
9. **Blog-comment batching:** Lives only on branch `old`; not promoted in v3.

---

You may use, copy, modify, merge, publish, and distribute this software, provided the copyright and permission notices are retained. The software is provided “as is”; see LICENSE for the full text.

---

## Disclaimer（免责声明）

- Search engines (including Google) have long discouraged **link schemes meant to manipulate rankings**. Short bursts of large-scale, low-relevance, or patterned backlinks can be treated as spam or trigger enforcement.
- Links are judged by quality and source; directory links vary widely. **Volume ≠ rankings.** This project **promises no** traffic or ranking outcomes.
- This repo is a workflow playbook — **not** a black-hat guide and not instructions on “how to evade” search actions.
- You are responsible for site behavior and outcomes from using this playbook; authors and maintainers accept no liability for loss.

Read the full page: [docs/disclaimer.md](docs/disclaimer.md). Official materials: [Google Search documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs) (official text wins).

---

**SagaSu** (@sujingshen) — indie building and product experiments.

- Twitter / X: [https://x.com/sujingshen](https://x.com/sujingshen)

# 🌻 Dandi API - Boilerplate for AI Micro SaaS Applications

**🤯 🤯 This repo was buikt with ENGLISH as the programming language with Cursor IDE and v0.🤯**


![Logo](https://github.com/emarco177/dandi/blob/main/public/demo.gif)

Dandi API is a comprehensive boilerplate repository for building AI-powered micro SaaS applications. It provides a solid foundation with essential components and functionalities needed to run an end-to-end micro SaaS application.

The service itself offers powerful insights, summaries, and analytics for open source GitHub repositories.

**🌐 Live Application: [https://www.dandi.cloud/](https://www.dandi.cloud/)**



## 🚀 Key Features

- **Complete Micro SaaS Structure**: Implements all necessary components for a fully functional AI micro SaaS application.
- **API Key Management**: Built-in system for handling API keys, UI heavily inspired by [Tavily](https://www.tavily.com/).
- **Rate Limiting**: Integrated rate limiting for API protection.
- **SSO Login**: Implemented Single Sign-On functionality.
- **AI Integration**: Leverages LangChain JS for AI capabilities.

## 🛠️ Built with Cursor IDE and v0

This entire project was developed using [Cursor IDE](https://cursor.com/), primarily through prompting with Cursor Composer and [v0](https://v0.dev/) . As a developer without frontend or full-stack experience, this project demonstrates the power of AI-assisted development.

**ENGLISH IS THE NEW PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE.**
[![udemy](https://img.shields.io/badge/Cursor%20Udemy%20Course-%20Coupon%20%2412.99-brightgreen)](https://www.udemy.com/course/cursor-ai-ide/?couponCode=APRIL-2026)

## 🧰 Tech Stack (TBH, Cursor did it all for me)

- **Frontend**: React, Next.js 13 (App Router), Tailwind CSS
- **Backend**: Node.js, Next.js API Routes
- **Database**: Supabase (PostgreSQL)
- **Authentication**: NextAuth.js
- **UI Components**: Shadcn UI, Radix UI
- **API**: RESTful API with rate limiting and API key authentication
- **AI**: LangChain JS 🦜🔗
- **Deployment**: Vercel 



## 🚀 Getting Started

To run this project locally, follow these steps:

1. Clone the repository:
   ```
   git clone https://github.com/emarco177/dandi.git
   cd dandi
   ```

2. Install dependencies:
   ```
   yarn install
   ```

3. Set up environment variables:
   Create a `.env.local` file in the root directory and add the necessary environment variables (refer to the Environment Variables section below).

4. Run the development server:
   ```
   yarn dev
   ```

5. Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000) in your browser to see the application.

## 🔐 Environment Variables

Create a `.env.local` file in the root directory with the following variables:

```
DB_URL=

NEXTAUTH_SECRET=
NEXTAUTH_URL=
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=
```

Note: Keep your `.env.local` file secure and never commit it to version control.

To build the project for production:

```
yarn build
```

To run the production build locally:

***S**imple **I**nventory **M**anagement and **P**roduct **L**ogistics* ![image](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=view&id=1WliiC62IAnbRIjaCLDmnzPm820IfNJJl) ## **Mockups**
## **Overall Summary**

SIMPL is a micro-SaaS application that is designed to improve the efficiency and maintainability of small and medium-sized businesses’ inventory and asset management capabilities. SIMPL does this by harnessing the power of Material UI, the Google Dart codebase, the Google Flutter framework, and the Google Firebase real-time database solution to provide a streamlined, simplistic, and elegant approach to inventory management and product logistics. Some primary use cases in which SIMPL excels is verifying and storing employee information, sharing databases between employees using invite-only security measures, generating QR codes for easy item tagging and tracking, scanning an item’s QR code to perform basic inventory tasks such as viewing item details, incrementing or decrementing item quantity, and building inventory reconciliation sheets. SIMPL also generates charts tracking item quantity over time, as well as store sales, so that users can make informed decisions about which products are high performers and which products simply cut into profit margins. Furthermore, SIMPL supports importing and exporting inventory data in CSV file format for further data manipulation in popular applications such as Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets.

## **What is the problem?**

In many small and medium-sized companies, inventory management is a burdensome and tedious task. Because of their size, many of these companies are unable to afford many of the more prominent inventory management applications, like Cin7 and Zoho. Furthermore, they have no need for many of the features that these applications provide, such as ecommerce integration, aftership tracking, serial number tracking, etc. These business owners simply need a way to keep track of what is in stock, what isn’t, and which items are providing the most profit. I saw this first-hand at the company I interned with in Summer 2021. Inventory reconciliation was being done by hand with paper every day. Employees would physically count the items on the shelves and mark the totals on paper to compare with what the online inventory was showing. When I asked the store supervisor about the reasoning behind hand-counting inventory, she said that she was unable to find a suitable software solution. As I began to research this issue further, trying to see if I could find a software alternative, I also started reading articles about how the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic had many reconsidering their job prospects, and how this was spurring the Great Resignation, which has led to an outgrowth of entrepreneurship and the creation of many small businesses. According to the Census Bureau, more than 4.4 million new businesses were created in the U.S. during 2020 alone. Pulling inspiration from my conversation with my supervisor, and the research I had done around inventory management software solutions, I saw a niche market and the idea of SIMPL was born. This new market of fledgling business owners and entrepreneurs has untapped potential in the realm of inventory management software, and SIMPL aims to be the answer.

## **How does SIMPL solve it?**

SIMPL will provide a service that many small and medium-sized business owners will benefit greatly from, without having to rely on any outside partnerships or external relationships. Using QR code technology in conjunction with the SIMPL app on iPhones, Androids, or Web-based devices, businesses will be able to manage their inventory in a quick and cost-efficient manner. Because SIMPL is cross-platform, it will be able to quickly integrate into a company’s workflow regardless of whether they use Apple, Android, or the Web-based devices. Also, because of CSV export capabilities, inventory data obtained through SIMPL can be shared and further analyzed through other applications if the user chooses to do so. This makes SIMPL a great addon for businesses that already have some form of inventory management in place, while also providing a competitive alternative for those who are in the market for a completely new system. SIMPL was built predominantly for phones, because we wanted to provide a cost-efficient solution for companies that didn’t want to invest in barcode scanner hardware and software. Utilizing QR code technology, as opposed to conventional barcodes, information retention capacity is greatly increased, being that a QR code has up to up to a 30% error correction capability. This means that up to 30% of the QR code can be damaged, by fading, dirt, accidental marking, scuffs, etc. and SIMPL can still read the information stored in the code. As inventory is moved between locations and endures the wear and tear of retail, this will reduce the headache that comes with inventory becoming unscannable due to damage to the barcode. Additionally, due to the more compact form of QR codes, printing costs may be decreased by up to 25% in certain use cases. Concerning logistics, SIMPL is designed to simplify communication first and foremost. Users will be able to see who last interacted with any item currently in the database. They will also be able to quickly and easily share stores with other users. Along with customary item insertion and deletion, SIMPL is designed to store scan-in and scan-out data for each item, allowing the application to generate detailed graphs concerning item quantity over a period of hours, days, months, or a year. For each store, SIMPL will also highlight which items are low in stock and which items are most popular, which will aid the user in making informed decisions about what items to purchase in the future. SIMPL also features an inventory reconciliation scan option, which will allow the user to scan the product on the physical store shelves, export that data to a separate CSV, and then compare the Official Inventory CSV to the Inventory Reconciliation CSV in order to find discrepancies quickly.

## **Who is the Target Market?**

Right now, our target market includes small to medium-sized retail companies, employing anywhere from 1 employee to 1000 employees, that either do not have an inventory management system in place, or would like to integrate a lightweight, cost-efficient addition into their current inventory management processes. With smaller businesses especially, there is a need to keep costs low. In doing so, more money can be put back into the business in the form of inventory and advertising, allowing the business to expand its profit margin and market presence. SIMPL is a solution for businesses who need inventory management and product logistics on a budget. As businesses reach those higher profit margins and bigger customer bases, inventory management becomes increasingly more important. Built with this in mind, SIMPL helps businesses establish a baseline for good inventory management practices early on, without divesting key funding that should be going to promote the business’s overall growth. We think that this affordability factor will be the main draw for customers who want to purchase and use the SIMPL software. Also, because of SIMPL’s availability on the major technology platforms (Web, Android, and iOS) we aim to be compatible with most, if not all, of the devices currently in use in our target market. Beyond our primary customer segment in retail , we would eventually like to bring SIMPL to small manufacturing companies and build a material requirement planning feature into the app, but that will depend on future development.

## **What is SIMPL's competitive advantage?**

There are a few other inventory management apps currently in the market, but, to our knowledge, none provide cross-platform support, an updated UI built to Google Material UI standards, an inventory reconciliation feature, and other streamlined features built specific to small and medium-sized businesses at a competitive price point. Many full-fledged software solutions and competitors, like Cin7, Ordoro, and Webgility, suffer from feature bloat and contain many tools that starting entrepreneurs and business owners may not need. SIMPL challenges the assumption that all of these extra features are necessary for an efficient management solution. Our research showed that features that generated Bill of Materials, Manufacturing Orders, or Purchase Orders, or integrated Point of Sale systems, were often under-utilized by many smaller business customers. Many of these bigger software options also lacked mobile apps to serve in the place of scanning hardware. Concerning the lightweight app sphere, we found that current apps such as Sortly, TookStock, and Telesto were very uniform in function, and there was not much to differentiate between them. None of these apps allowed users to see change in quantity over time graphically. Sortly was the only application that allowed QR code scanning, while TookStock was the only app that offered a semblance of inventory reconciliation. SIMPL provides these niche features while also covering the standard basics of item cataloging, item insertion/deletion, store insertion/deletion, and store share features. There seems to be an assumption that these are the only features necessary for smaller business owners. However, the entrepreneurial spirit continues to expand as COVID-19 restrictions lift and people become increasingly more independent, and they are looking for smarter and better ways to work. These future innovators and business creators need a way to manage their inventory without getting bogged down in feature bloat while still being able to integrate newer inventory technologies like QR codes, and see data in a visual way with graphs and charts. Current options in the app market don’t provide all of these features in one package, and SIMPL can fill in that gap.

Strava-Tool ===========



> A personal side project with Strava API using Python. --- ### Motivation This project is my personal side project with Strava API. The goal of this project is to analyze my training data for better future performance, as well as to **hone my Data Analysis & Visualization skills**. The idea was originally coming from the fact that my increasing demands for uploading indoor cycling activity data to Strava, especially in the lockdown time of COVID-19. I usually did indoor training with Zwift during the weekdays and long weekend group ride on the weekend. When training indoors with Zwift, I used to also record my cycling workout with a bicycle computer, for more workout information like power zone, laps, time, etc. This means there will be two generated files pointing to the same activity in the end. If you have authorized Zwift to connect with Strava beforehand, each of your virtual ride data will be AUTOMATICALLY synchronized to Strava. That's really exciting and satisfying when you saw a Strava notification telling you that "Your activity is ready." after suffering on the saddle for hours. (You know that feeling.😉) However, as an engineering graduate student and bike🚴 enthusiast, I decided to to take more control over the whole interaction process with Strava, in order to know what's happening under the hood. Therefore, I disabled the connection between the two Apps, and started developing a toy StravaAutoUploader tool with Python as the starting point of this side project. Hopefully it could be someday extended to have some advanced features like Golden Cheetah, TrainingPeaks, for analyzing, tracking, and predicting my performance on the bike!

--- ### Features (__just name a few, not completed yet__) - Fixing and uploading workout (Ride, Virtual Ride, Run, Hike, etc.) activity files with the help of batch script automation using Task Scheduler (Windows) https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/43208378/126695209-51a2c492-9b8d-4668-808d-801e813fe502.mp4 https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/43208378/126695221-0dcaaa7f-4b31-4093-ad5f-548504a6f335.mp4 - Analyzing workout data using Pandas package e.g., - yearly summary (similar to [Strava Year in Sport Data Report](https://blog.strava.com/press/yis2020/)) - How many workout activities I did per month/week in a year? - How much time I spent on cycling activities per month/week in a year? - etc. - Visualizing workout data using Seaborn and Matplotlib libraries as well as Tableau software e.g., - heatmap - etc. --- ### How to use the code * [ ] Pipenv * [ ] https://selenium-python.readthedocs.io/installation.html#drivers * [ ] batch file * [ ] auth * [ ] config --- ### Good resources - Getting started with Strava API: - [Getting Started With The Strava API: A Tutorial](https://medium.com/@annthurium/getting-started-with-the-strava-api-a-tutorial-f3909496cd2d) - [YouTube Playlist "Strava API for Beginners", by Fran Polignano](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLO6KswO64zVvcRyk0G0MAzh5oKMLb6rTW) - Further development ideas: [Strava Labs](https://labs.strava.com/) - [Strava API Developer Forum](https://groups.google.com/g/strava-api) --- ### Support the project Whether you use this project, have learned something from it, or just like it, please consider supporting it by buying me a coffee or making one-time donations via PayPal, so I can dedicate more time on open-source projects like this. 💪🙃 Thanks!:heart: and Cheers!:beers: --- ### Contact If you have any question or suggestion, feel free to contact me at huaming.huang.tw@gmail.com. Contributions are also welcomed. Please open a [pull-request](https://github.com/huaminghuangtw/Strava-Tool/compare) or an [issue](https://github.com/huaminghuangtw/Strava-Tool/issues/new) in this repository. --- ### License This project is licensed under the terms of [![MIT](https://img.shields.io/github/license/huaminghuangtw/Strava-Tool.svg?style=flat-square&label=License&colorB=black)](./LICENSE).
